critic.verdict: The pull-back clearly serves the journey: it opens tight on the boy and bucket on the walkway, then reveals the full kampong and outhouse destination as the locked-together boy and bucket drift up-right and shrink slightly with distance. Both cut-outs stay coherent with no tearing, ghosting, doubled edges or awkward frame clipping, and the final near-full-frame view is a strong image to dwell on. The 1950s lithograph character is retained.

rounds.verdict: A coherent, era-appropriate pull-back with the boy and bucket held together, but the travel toward the outhouse is too small to clearly tell the scene's story and the standpipe is clipped throughout, including the final hold.
filmIssues: The pull-back is visible but timid: across the six frames the framing, boy position and scale change only slightly, so the clip reads as little more than a slow plain pull-back rather than a purposeful journey toward the outhouse.

The boy's walk is not clearly legible. His drift right/up is small, and his 0.92 end scale combined with the camera pull-back makes him shrink without a strong sense of travelling along the plank walkway toward the teal outhouse on the right.

The foreground standpipe at left is awkwardly clipped by the frame edge in every frame, including the final dwell frame, despite being fully inside the plate; the final pan right keeps it cropped instead of settling on a clean wide kampong picture.

Boy and bucket do stay together with identical drift/scale and no visible tearing, doubled edges or ghost on the pale ground; the halftone-shimmer is fitting and subtle for the 1950s offset-lithograph style.
